title: Project 5: contact book using dynamic memory
learningObjectives: Explain the topic and its C rules.
Trace the example and identify its purpose.
Identify important validation and failure cases.

understand.concept: A contact book stores a variable number of contacts, supports search and deletion, and releases every allocation. A design may use a resizable array of structures or a linked list.
understand.whyItMatters: This project exercises allocation, resizing, string ownership, search and cleanup discipline.
understand.analogy: Treat the project or language feature as a set of components with explicit interfaces and responsibilities.

explain.narrative:
A contact book stores a variable number of contacts, supports search and deletion, and releases every allocation. A design may use a resizable array of structures or a linked list.

For a complete implementation, define input constraints, ownership, error handling and test cases before coding. Compile with warnings and verify normal, boundary and failure behaviour.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: calloc allocates storage for two Contact objects and initializes their bytes to zero. It does not allocate the strings referenced by the pointer members; a complete implementation must allocate, validate and free those strings separately.

practise.guidedTask: Draw the contact array and its separately owned name and phone strings.
practise.independentTask: Implement add, search, update and delete while documenting ownership and handling partial allocation failures.
hints: A zeroed pointer member is a null pointer on ordinary hosted implementations, but initialize and manage pointer members according to C rules and project portability.
Free each owned string before releasing the containing array.
A shallow structure copy duplicates pointer values, not the pointed-to strings.
